newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore bank interim net growth seen over 14 pct.
newsitem.headline: Singapore bank interim net growth seen over 14 pct.

text.p: Singapore's four main banks are likely to report net profit rises in excess of 14 percent for the first half of 1997, analysts said on Thursday.
The four -- Development Bank of Singapore, Overseas-Chinese Banking Corp, Overseas Union Bank and United Overseas Bank -- face declining loans growth and provisions for bad overseas loans this year.
But most of the impact of these factors will come in the second half and analysts are confident the sector will shine when interim results are published over the next few weeks.
"The first half will be okay, but the second half will be more difficult," said Kevin Scully, banks analyst at Schroders.
Singapore's banks face a steady decline in loans growth.
This averaged around 16 percent last year as customers borrowed on the back of pay-packets inflated by several years of heady economic expansion.

But Singapore's economy has hit a rocky patch over the past year. A slowdown in its key electronics industry -- which accounts for about half its industrial output -- and a slump in the property market have trimmed consumer spending.

After peaking at almost 20 percent year-on-year at the end of 1996, loans growth has fallen steadily this year to around 13 percent in April and is expected to average 12 percent for 1997 and maybe as little as seven percent in 1998.
"A large part of bank loan assets still come from the domestic market," said Tan Lai Peng, banking analyst at DBS Securities.
She said the banks had expanded regionally in recent years and the impact of slowing loans growth for some of them would be moderated by foreign lending.
"Banks with strong overseas operations will continue to benefit," she said.

OUB, in particular, was likely to gain from its exposure to the Malaysian and Hong Kong markets. She forecast OUB first-half net profit growth at around 20 percent above the Singapore $142.15 million (US$98.7 million) reported a year ago.
For the full-year 1997, Edinburgh Financial Publishing's Estimate Directory (TED), which polled 33 analysts, sees OUB's net profit up by around 19 percent to S$309.5 million.
Analysts say the banks are likely to put higher provisions for bad debts into the first half but this would be balanced by a traditional desire to impress in the first six months.
Scully said DBS, Singapore's biggest bank in terms of assets, would probably show a net profit rise of slightly more than the 12 percent TED sees for the whole of 1997.
This would put DBS's interim net profit around S$360 million, up from S$316.95 million a year ago.
OCBC, another bank with big expansion plans outside Singapore, is widely expected to report a 13-16 percent net profit gain from the S$304.58 million for first-half 1996.
UOB, which made a net profit of S$352.73 million a year ago, is seen coming in with a 12-13 percent year-on-year rise.
Most analysts like the sector as a whole, with many seeing OUB's aggressive drive for business outside Singapore as offering attractive future growth prospects.
Violet Soh, analyst at Fraser Securities, prefers the other three in terms of valuations and tips their foreign tranches.
